claim: Ataxin-2 (Atx2) is a translational control molecule mutated in spinocerebellar ataxia type II and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: Ataxin-2 (Atx2) is a translational control molecule mutated in spinocerebellar ataxia type II and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Atx2's role in disease, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Intrinsically disordered domains (IDRs) of Atx2 facilitate mRNP condensation into granules.
source: While intrinsically disordered domains (IDRs) of Atx2 facilitate mRNP condensation into granules, how IDRs work with structured domains to enable positive and negative regulation of target mRNAs remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited in the manuscript and confirmed by the current study's findings.

claim: TRIBE technology was used to identify an extensive data set of Atx2-target mRNAs in the Drosophila brain and S2 cells.
source: Using the Targets of RNA-Binding Proteins Identified by Editing technology, we identified an extensive data set of Atx2-target mRNAs in the Drosophila brain and S2 cells.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach and presents the resulting data.

claim: Atx2 interactions with AU-rich elements in 3′UTRs appear to modulate stability/turnover of a large fraction of target mRNAs.
source: Atx2 interactions with AU-rich elements in 3′UTRs appear to modulate stability/turnover of a large fraction of these target mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by TRIBE data showing ARE enrichment and RNAseq data showing mRNA level changes upon Atx2 knockdown.

claim: Atx2 interacts closely with target mRNAs within mRNP granules.
source: These findings increase the understanding of neuronal translational control mechanisms and inform strategies for Atx2-based interventions under development for neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cIDR deletion, which prevents granule formation, also prevents mRNA editing.

claim: Atx2 contains distinct protein domains that drive or oppose RNP-granule assembly.
source: Atx2 (1) interacts closely with target mRNAs within mRNP granules, (2) contains distinct protein domains that drive or oppose RNP-granule assembly, and (3) has additional essential roles outside of mRNP granules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by domain deletion experiments showing cIDR drives and Lsm opposes granule assembly.

claim: Atx2 has additional essential roles outside of mRNP granules.
source: Atx2 (1) interacts closely with target mRNAs within mRNP granules, (2) contains distinct protein domains that drive or oppose RNP-granule assembly, and (3) has additional essential roles outside of mRNP granules.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that structured domains are essential for viability but not required for TRIBE-target binding.

claim: Ataxin-2 positively or negatively regulates the translation of specific mRNAs.
source: At a molecular level, Ataxin-2 positively or negatively regulates the translation of specific mRNAs (Lee et al., 2017; Lim and Allada, 2013; McCann et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Ataxin-2 mediates the assembly of mRNPs into cytoplasmic mRNP granules visible in resting neurons or in RNA stress granules.
source: At the same time, the protein mediates the assembly of mRNPs into cytoplasmic mRNP granules visible in resting neurons or in RNA stress granules (SGs) that occur in most cells in response to stress (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018; Bentmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and confirmed by the current work.

claim: Ataxin-2 contributes to cell viability and differentiation as well as cellular responses to viral, ER, heat-, and oxidative stress.
source: At a cellular level, Ataxin-2 contributes to cell viability and differentiation as well as cellular responses to viral, ER, heat-, and oxidative stress (Bonenfant et al., 2019; Del Castillo et al., 2019; Ralser et al., 2005; van de Loo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Ataxin-2 regulates metabolism, circadian rhythm, and the consolidation of long-term memory.
source: Finally, at an organismal level, the protein regulates metabolism, circadian rhythm, and the consolidation of long-term memory (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018; Lim and Allada, 2013; Meierhofer et al., 2016; Pfeffer et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Genetic mutations in human Ataxin-2 (Atxn2) can cause spinocerebellar ataxia type II or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Parallel clinical genetic studies have shown that genetic mutations in human Ataxin-2 (Atxn2) can cause the hereditary neurodegenerative diseases spinocerebellar ataxia type II or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Daoud et al., 2011; Elden et al., 2010; Lastres-Becker et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2011; Scoles and Pulst, 2018; Wadia, 1977; Wadia and Swami, 1971)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited clinical genetic studies.

claim: Genetic reduction of Ataxin-2 activity slows neurodegeneration in animal models of ALS.
source: subsequent work showing that genetic reduction of Ataxin-2 activity slows neurodegeneration in animal models of ALS has inspired the design and development of therapeutics targeting human Ataxin-2 (Becker et al., 2017; Becker and Gitler, 2018; Elden et al., 2010; Scoles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies in animal models.

claim: Intrinsically disordered domains (IDRs) present on RNA-binding proteins contribute to macromolecular condensation or liquid–liquid phase separation reactions.
source: The above biological and clinical studies of Ataxin-2 are connected by the insight that intrinsically disordered domains (IDRs) present on RNA-binding proteins contribute to macromolecular condensation or liquid–liquid phase separation reactions, wherein monomeric units form dynamic assemblies held together by weak multivalent interactions (Jain and Vale, 2017; Kato and McKnight, 2018; Murray et al., 2017; Saha and Hyman, 2017; Van Treeck et al., 2018; Van Treeck and Parker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on phase separation.

claim: IDRs not only support assembly of mRNP granules but also are prone to assemble into amyloid-like fibers.
source: Significantly, IDRs not only support assembly of mRNP granules but also are prone to assemble into amyloid-like fibers.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on IDR behavior.

claim: Disease-causing mutations often increase the efficiency of amyloid formation, particularly within mRNP granules where the RNA-binding proteins are concentrated.
source: Disease-causing mutations often increase the efficiency of amyloid formation, particularly within mRNP granules where the RNA-binding proteins are concentrated (Courchaine et al., 2016; Kato et al., 2012; Lim and Allada, 2013; Nedelsky and Taylor, 2019; Patel et al., 2015; Ramaswami et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies on disease mutations and amyloid formation.

claim: The domain structure of Ataxin-2 is highly conserved across species.
source: The domain structure of Ataxin-2 is highly conserved across species, with N-terminal Like-Sm (Lsm) and Lsm-associated (LsmAD) domains, a more carboxy-terminal polyA binding protein interaction motif 2 (PAM2) domain, as well as strongly disordered regions (respectively mIDR and cIDR) in the middle and C-terminal regions of the protein (Albrecht et al., 2004, Satterfield and Pallanck, 2006; Nonhoff et al., 2007; Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural studies.

claim: Each structured domain of Atx2 is essential for normal viability in Drosophila.
source: Specifically, while each structured domain is essential for normal viability, the IDR domains are not.
evidence: This is based on genetic studies in Drosophila cited in the manuscript.

claim: The IDR domains of Atx2 are not essential for normal viability in Drosophila.
source: Specifically, while each structured domain is essential for normal viability, the IDR domains are not.
evidence: This is based on genetic studies in Drosophila cited in the manuscript.

claim: The cIDR of Atx2 is required for normal mRNP assembly and long-term memory.
source: However, the cIDR is required for normal mRNP assembly and long-term memory as well as for facilitating cytotoxicity in Drosophila Fus and C9orf72 models for ALS/FTD (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The cIDR of Atx2 facilitates cytotoxicity in Drosophila Fus and C9orf72 models for ALS/FTD.
source: However, the cIDR is required for normal mRNP assembly and long-term memory as well as for facilitating cytotoxicity in Drosophila Fus and C9orf72 models for ALS/FTD (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: TRIBE reproducibly identifies RNA binding protein (RBP) target mRNAs in vivo.
source: To identify in vivo targets of Atx2 in Drosophila melanogaster brain, we used TRIBE, a technology previously shown to reproducibly identify RNA binding protein (RBP) target mRNAs in vivo (McMahon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study describing the TRIBE method.

claim: Transgenic flies expressing Atx2-ADARcd were generated for TRIBE analysis.
source: We generated transgenic flies that express Atx2 linked to the catalytic domain of Drosophila RNA-modifying enzyme adenosine deaminase (ADARcd) at the carboxy terminal along with a V5 epitope tag under the control of the Gal4-responsive UAS promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: In tissue expressing the Atx2-ADARcd transgene, mRNAs undergo adenosine-to-inosine editing specifically at positions proximal to Atx2 binding sites.
source: In tissue expressing the Atx2-ADARcd transgene, mRNAs should undergo adenosine-to-inosine editing specifically at positions proximal to Atx2 binding sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is the principle of the TRIBE method applied in this study.

claim: Atx2-ADARcd is expressed specifically in the nervous system using elav-Gal4.
source: In an elav-Gal4 background, where the Gal4 transcription factor is expressed in postmitotic neurons, Atx2-ADARcd is expressed specifically in the nervous system.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for tissue-specific expression.

claim: Temperature-sensitive Gal80ts was used to temporally restrict neural expression to adult flies.
source: We further temporally restricted neural expression to adult flies with the use of the temperature-sensitive Gal4 inhibitor, GAL80ts, that is active at temperatures below 18°C.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for temporal control of expression.

claim: 528 and 481 edit sites were identified in independent replicates of the TRIBE experiment.
source: Of the 528 and 481 edit sites represented in independent replicates, at least 317 were common to both samples, demonstrating the reproducibility of the experiments (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: 317 edit sites were common to both TRIBE replicates.
source: Of the 528 and 481 edit sites represented in independent replicates, at least 317 were common to both samples, demonstrating the reproducibility of the experiments (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments demonstrating reproducibility.

claim: The 317 common edits could be assigned to 256 unique genes.
source: These 317 common edits could be assigned to 256 unique genes, with the majority of genes only being edited at a single site (215 genes, 67.8% of edits) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: The majority of Atx2-target genes (215 genes, 67.8%) were edited at a single site.
source: These 317 common edits could be assigned to 256 unique genes, with the majority of genes only being edited at a single site (215 genes, 67.8% of edits) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: Atx2-target mRNAs were distributed across the brain transcriptome irrespective of mRNA abundance.
source: The Atx2-target mRNAs were distributed across the brain transcriptome irrespective of the abundance of an mRNA indicating that edits were not random events, but rather reflect sequence- and structure-specific association of these mRNAs with Atx2-ADARcd (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments showing specificity of binding.

claim: Edits in Adipokinetic hormone (Akh) and 14-3-3 epsilon mRNAs were validated by Sanger sequencing.
source: For instance, Sanger sequencing confirmed that edits in Adipokinetic hormone (Akh) and 14-3-3 epsilon mRNAs occur at identified sites, with efficiencies indicated by TRIBE analysis (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is validation data confirming TRIBE results.

claim: Atx2 associates with specific RNA motifs present on targets identified by TRIBE analyses from fly brain.
source: Taken together, the data indicates that Atx2 associates with specific RNA motifs present on targets identified by TRIBE analyses from fly brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TRIBE data and validation experiments.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of Atx2 targets indicated particular enrichment of mRNAs encoding neuropeptides and hormones.
source: A Gene Ontology analysis of Atx2 targets (Table 1) indicated particular enrichment of mRNAs encoding neuropeptides and hormones, as well as mRNAs encoding monoamine transporters, ion channels, and vesicle transport proteins.
evidence: This is data from Gene Ontology analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of Atx2 targets indicated enrichment of mRNAs encoding monoamine transporters, ion channels, and vesicle transport proteins.
source: A Gene Ontology analysis of Atx2 targets (Table 1) indicated particular enrichment of mRNAs encoding neuropeptides and hormones, as well as mRNAs encoding monoamine transporters, ion channels, and vesicle transport proteins.
evidence: This is data from Gene Ontology analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: Atx2 interactions occurred predominantly within 3′UTRs of target mRNAs (69.5%).
source: By converting the TRIBE edits into metagene coordinates, we found that Atx2 interactions occurred predominantly within 3′UTRs of target mRNAs (69.5%), while the coding region (CDS) and 5′UTR accounted for 26.7% and 4% of edits, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from metagene analysis of TRIBE edits.

claim: The coding region (CDS) and 5′UTR accounted for 26.7% and 4% of Atx2 edits, respectively.
source: By converting the TRIBE edits into metagene coordinates, we found that Atx2 interactions occurred predominantly within 3′UTRs of target mRNAs (69.5%), while the coding region (CDS) and 5′UTR accounted for 26.7% and 4% of edits, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is data from metagene analysis of TRIBE edits.

claim: All identified edits occurred almost exclusively in exons.
source: All the identified edits occurred almost exclusively in exons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), which might be due to polyA selection causing experimental bias or that Atx2 binds to only mature mRNA in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: Edits within CDS were often accompanied by edits in the 3′UTR of the same mRNA.
source: Edits within CDS were often accompanied by edits in the 3′UTR of the same mRNA, further indicating a key role for Atx2–3′UTR interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: Atx2 edit sites were particularly prevalent in brain transcripts with longer 3′UTRs.
source: Also pointing to a role in 3′UTR regulation, Atx2 edit sites were particularly prevalent in brain transcripts with longer 3′UTRs that are more often subject to translational control (Inagaki et al., 2020; Miura et al., 2013; Wang and Yi, 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments and cited studies on 3′UTR regulation.

claim: An AU-rich element (ARE) 'UAUAUAUA' was identified as highly enriched in mRNA target sequences within 100 bases of identified edit sites.
source: Further analyses using the MEME suite of tools for motif-based sequence analysis identified an AU-rich element (ARE) 'UAUAUAUA' as highly enriched in mRNA target sequences within 100 bases of identified edit sites (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is data from motif analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: AREs are most abundant near 3′UTR edit sites of the target mRNAs.
source: These AREs, previously implicated in the regulation of mRNA stability, are most abundant near 3′UTR edits sites of the target mRNAs, while a secondary motif with GC-rich sequence was found predominantly for the CDS edits (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from motif analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: A secondary motif with GC-rich sequence was found predominantly for the CDS edits.
source: These AREs, previously implicated in the regulation of mRNA stability, are most abundant near 3′UTR edits sites of the target mRNAs, while a secondary motif with GC-rich sequence was found predominantly for the CDS edits (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is data from motif analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: The ARE motifs in the 3′UTR are conserved between closely related Drosophila species for Vmat and Akh genes.
source: A multiple-sequence alignment for two of the genes (Vmat and Akh) shows the motifs in the 3′UTR are conserved between closely related Drosophila species (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is data from sequence alignment analysis.

claim: AREs are major cis-regulatory motifs in the 3′UTR of mRNAs that regulate their stability.
source: AREs are major cis-regulatory motifs in the 3′UTR of mRNAs that regulate their stability (Otsuka et al., 2019; Vasudevan and Peltz, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited studies.

claim: Several RBPs modulate mRNA stability by binding to AREs and regulating their accessibility to RNA degradative machinery.
source: For this reason, several RBPs modulate mRNA stability by binding to AREs and regulating their accessibility to RNA degradative machinery (Mayya and Duchaine, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a cited study.

claim: Pumilio binding to ARE increases mRNA degradation.
source: For example, Pumilio binding to ARE increases degradation, while HuR binding stabilizes the mRNAs (López de Silanes et al., 2004; Weidmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited studies.

claim: HuR binding to ARE stabilizes mRNAs.
source: For example, Pumilio binding to ARE increases degradation, while HuR binding stabilizes the mRNAs (López de Silanes et al., 2004; Weidmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by cited studies.

claim: RNAseq data confirmed partial knockdown of Atx2 mRNA in experimental flies expressing Atx2-RNAi.
source: RNAseq data confirmed partial knockdown of Atx2 mRNA in experimental flies expressing Atx2-RNAi (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments.

claim: Atx2 levels were reduced only in Gal4-expressing cells in the wing disc compared to neighboring control cells.
source: Atx2 levels were down only in the Gal4-expressing cells compared to the neighboring control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from immunostaining experiments validating RNAi efficiency.

claim: Atx2 knockdown caused a significant reduction in levels of over 53.2% of the Atx2-target mRNAs.
source: Atx2 knockdown caused a significant reduction in levels of over 53.2% of the Atx2-target mRNAs, indicating a broad role for Atx2 in target-mRNA stabilization (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments following Atx2 knockdown.

claim: The levels of ~8.8% of the Atx2-target mRNAs were increased with Atx2 knockdown.
source: This was, however, not universal, and we observed that the levels of ~8.8% of the target mRNAs were increased with Atx2 knockdown.
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments following Atx2 knockdown.

claim: ~22.5% of all mRNAs from the global brain transcriptome were reduced by Atx2 knockdown.
source: Non-target mRNA levels were substantially less affected: ~22.5% of all mRNAs from the global brain transcriptome were reduced by Atx2 knockdown, with ~57.2% showing no detectable change in expression levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments following Atx2 knockdown.

claim: ~57.2% of all mRNAs from the global brain transcriptome showed no detectable change in expression levels following Atx2 knockdown.
source: Non-target mRNA levels were substantially less affected: ~22.5% of all mRNAs from the global brain transcriptome were reduced by Atx2 knockdown, with ~57.2% showing no detectable change in expression levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments following Atx2 knockdown.

claim: The analysis of nascent transcripts using intron reads showed that predominant Atx2 targets (~85%) remain unchanged.
source: In contrast, the analysis of nascent transcripts using intron reads showed that predominant Atx2 targets (~85%) remain unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the downregulation of target mRNAs in Atx2 RNAi is posttranscriptional.
evidence: This is data from intron read analysis.

claim: The downregulation of target mRNAs in Atx2 RNAi is posttranscriptional.
source: In contrast, the analysis of nascent transcripts using intron reads showed that predominant Atx2 targets (~85%) remain unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the downregulation of target mRNAs in Atx2 RNAi is posttranscriptional.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that nascent transcripts are unchanged while mature mRNA levels are reduced.

claim: Atx2-ADARcd edited ~179 mRNA targets preferentially in the 3′UTR in S2 cells.
source: Atx2-ADARcd edited ~179 mRNA targets preferentially in the 3′UTR in S2 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments in S2 cells.

claim: The targets identified from S2 cell TRIBE only marginally overlapped with the targets identified in the Drosophila brain.
source: The targets identified from S2 cell TRIBE only marginally overlapped with the targets identified in the Drosophila brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is data comparing TRIBE results from brain and S2 cells.

claim: Atx2 silencing in S2 cells caused reduction in the levels of significant percentage of targets (~49%) compared to ~14% of total S2 transcripts.
source: Like in brain, Atx2 silencing in S2 cells caused reduction in the levels of significant percentage of targets (~49%) compared to ~14% of total S2 transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A, B).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments in S2 cells following Atx2 knockdown.

claim: ~74% of targets that showed reduced expression in Atx2 RNAi were upregulated in Atx2 overexpression in S2 cells.
source: In contrast, ~74% of targets that showed reduced expression in Atx2 RNAi were upregulated in Atx2 overexpression (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is data from RNAseq experiments in S2 cells comparing Atx2 knockdown and overexpression.

claim: UTRs with high AREScore are clearly enriched in the Atx2-target mRNAs compared to the general neural transcriptome.
source: In support of a broad role for Atx2 in the regulation of ARE function in neurons, UTRs with high AREScore are clearly enriched in the Atx2-target mRNAs compared to the general neural transcriptome (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is data from AREScore analysis.

claim: Within the group of Atx2-target RNAs identified by TRIBE, higher AREScore strongly predict mRNAs whose steady-state levels are reduced by Atx2 knockdown in brain and S2 cells.
source: Further, within the group of Atx2-target RNAs identified by TRIBE, higher AREScore strongly predict mRNAs whose steady-state levels are reduced by Atx2 knockdown in brain and S2 cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is data from AREScore analysis combined with RNAseq data.

claim: Atx2 stabilizes a subset of its target mRNAs by binding to AREs.
source: These results indicate that Atx2 stabilizes a subset of its target mRNAs by binding to AREs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AREScore and RNAseq data.

claim: Lsm+LsmAD domains on their own could not efficiently target ADAR to mRNA.
source: Initial observations indicated that Lsm+LsmAD domains on their own could not efficiently target ADAR to mRNA: transcripts sequenced from Lsm+LsmAD-ADARcd-expressing brains contained negligible edits, which did not overlap significantly with Atx2 targets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with domain deletions.

claim: The Lsm and LsmAD domains are insufficient to drive Atx2–mRNA interactions in vivo.
source: Therefore, the Lsm and LsmAD domains are insufficient to drive Atx2–mRNA interactions in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TRIBE data with Lsm+LsmAD-ADARcd.

claim: Deletions of either Lsm or LsmAD did not block the ability of Atx2 to interact with most TRIBE targets.
source: Further, deletions of either Lsm or LsmAD did not block the ability of Atx2 to interact with most TRIBE targets: thus, they appear neither necessary nor sufficient for Atx2 targeting to these mRNAs (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with domain deletions.

claim: The Lsm and LsmAD domains appear neither necessary nor sufficient for Atx2 targeting to TRIBE-identified mRNAs.
source: Further, deletions of either Lsm or LsmAD did not block the ability of Atx2 to interact with most TRIBE targets: thus, they appear neither necessary nor sufficient for Atx2 targeting to these mRNAs (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TRIBE data with domain deletions.

claim: Deletion of cIDR abolished Atx2 binding to most target mRNAs.
source: In contrast to the effects of deleting the Lsm domain, deletion of cIDR abolished Atx2 binding to most target mRNAs (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with cIDR deletion.

claim: Atx2 moves into proximity of target mRNAs only after cIDR-mediated granule formation.
source: As the cIDR plays a major role in mRNP assembly (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018), this unexpected observation suggests that Atx2 moves into proximity of target mRNAs only after cIDR-mediated granule formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cIDR deletion prevents both granule formation and mRNA editing.

claim: Deletion of the mIDR resulted only in a relatively minor reduction in target binding.
source: Deletion of the mIDR resulted only in a relatively minor reduction in target binding, but this is consistent with prior work indicating only a minor role in mRNP assembly (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with mIDR deletion.

claim: The deletion of Lsm, LsmAD, or mIDR domains did not alter AU-rich motif preference for Atx2.
source: In addition, the deletion of Lsm, LsmAD, or mIDR domains did not alter AU-rich motif preference for Atx2, suggesting that these domains do not provide mRNA binding specificity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is data from motif analysis of TRIBE targets with domain deletions.

claim: Lsm-domain deletions resulted in a significantly larger number of edited target mRNAs compared to the full-length, wild-type Atx2.
source: A key observation is that while Lsm-domain deletions did not reduce RNA edits, they also curiously resulted in a significantly larger number of edited target mRNAs compared to the full-length, wild-type Atx2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with Lsm deletion.

claim: Several of the apparently novel targets of Atx2∆Lsm were also bound by the wild-type Atx2 but with reduced affinity.
source: A more detailed analysis showed that several of the apparently novel targets of Atx2∆Lsm were also bound by the wild-type Atx2 but with reduced affinity and were therefore below the threshold of our analysis (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is data from detailed analysis of TRIBE targets comparing wild-type and Lsm deletion.

claim: The Lsm domain acts to broadly antagonize physiologically relevant mRNA interactions driven by the cIDR.
source: Because sequencing depth, read quality, and ADAR mRNA and protein levels were similar across control and domain-deletion experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–C), these observations argue that the Lsm domain acts to broadly antagonize physiologically relevant mRNA interactions driven by the cIDR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TRIBE data with domain deletions.

claim: While the cIDR domain of Atx2 is essential for its mRNA target interactions, the Lsm domain is inhibitory.
source: Thus, while the cIDR domain of Atx2 is essential for its mRNA target interactions, the Lsm domain is inhibitory: in its absence, Atx2 shows an enhanced association with its native, target mRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TRIBE data with domain deletions.

claim: Expression of wild-type C-terminally SNAP tagged Atx2 (Atx2-SNAP) in S2 cells led to the formation of SG-like RNP-granule foci.
source: Expression of wild-type C-terminally SNAP tagged Atx2 (Atx2-SNAP) in S2 cells led to the formation of SG-like RNP-granule foci through a mechanism dependent on cIDR as described previously (Figure 5ii, v; Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is data from cell biological experiments with SNAP-tagged Atx2.

claim: Expression of Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP constructs lacking the Lsm domain induced significantly larger RNP granules compared to wild-type Atx2-SNAP.
source: Strikingly consistent with our predictions, expression of Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP constructs lacking the Lsm domain induced significantly larger RNP granules compared to wild-type Atx2-SNAP (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is data from cell biological experiments with Lsm-deleted Atx2.

claim: Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP-induced granules contained the SG protein, G3BP/Rasputin (Rin).
source: Similar to wild-type Atx2-SNAP granules, these large Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP-induced granules also contained the SG protein, G3BP/Rasputin (Rin) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and their formation required the presence the cIDR (Figure 5iv).
evidence: This is data from immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: The formation of Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP-induced granules required the presence of the cIDR.
source: Similar to wild-type Atx2-SNAP granules, these large Atx2∆Lsm-SNAP-induced granules also contained the SG protein, G3BP/Rasputin (Rin) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and their formation required the presence the cIDR (Figure 5iv).
evidence: This is data from cell biological experiments with double deletion constructs.

claim: The Lsm domain acts antagonistically to cIDR to prevent RNP granule assembly.
source: Thus, Lsm domain appears to act antagonistically to cIDR to prevent RNP granule assembly.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the granule formation experiments.

claim: Atx2 with two Lsm domains showed much smaller foci in S2 cells.
source: Remarkably, Atx2 with two Lsm showed much smaller foci in S2 cells (Figure 5Aiii).
evidence: This is data from cell biological experiments with 2XLsm Atx2.

claim: While ∆Lsm formed fewer but larger granules, increasing the valency of Lsm domains led to the formation of several smaller granules.
source: Quantification of granules in these cells reiterated that while ∆Lsm formed fewer but larger granules, increasing the valency of Lsm domains led to the formation of several smaller granules (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is data from quantification of granule size and number.

claim: Deletion of the Lsm enhances and addition of an extra Lsm domain inhibits RNP assembly.
source: Taken together, the observations that deletion of the Lsm enhances and addition of an extra Lsm domain inhibits RNP assembly provide strong support for two opposing activities encoded by the Lsm and cIDR domains of Atx2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the granule formation experiments.

claim: Atx2 functions in neurons as a translational activator of the period mRNA that controls circadian rhythms.
source: Previous work has shown that Drosophila Atx2 functions in neurons as a translational activator of the period mRNA that controls circadian rhythms and as a translational repressor of the calcium-calmodulin-dependent kinase CaMKII involved in synaptic plasticity and memory (Lim and Allada, 2013; Sudhakaran et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Atx2 functions as a translational repressor of the calcium-calmodulin-dependent kinase CaMKII involved in synaptic plasticity and memory.
source: Previous work has shown that Drosophila Atx2 functions in neurons as a translational activator of the period mRNA that controls circadian rhythms and as a translational repressor of the calcium-calmodulin-dependent kinase CaMKII involved in synaptic plasticity and memory (Lim and Allada, 2013; Sudhakaran et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Atx2 is required for the assembly of neuronal mRNPs believed to provide pools of synaptically localized mRNAs whose translation contributes to the consolidation of long-term memory.
source: Atx2 is also required for the assembly of neuronal mRNPs believed to provide pools of synaptically localized mRNAs whose translation contributes the consolidation of long-term memory (McCann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Specific positive and negative translational functions of Atx2 are mediated by structured–domain interactions with Lsm12 or Me31B/DDX6, respectively.
source: These studies indicate the specific positive and negative translational functions of Atx2, which are mediated by structured–domain interactions with Lsm12 or Me31B/DDX6, respectively (Lee et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: mRNP-assembly functions of Atx2 are mediated by its cIDR.
source: and that mRNP-assembly functions are mediated by its cIDR (Bakthavachalu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: TRIBE allows in vivo RNA targets of RBPs to be identified from small tissue samples, eliminating several technical challenges and artifacts associated with immunoprecipitation-based methods.
source: TRIBE allows in vivo RNA targets of RBPs to be identified from small tissue samples, eliminating several technical challenges and artifacts associated with immunoprecipitation-based methods (Jin et al., 2020; McMahon et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on the TRIBE method.

claim: 256 Drosophila brain mRNAs were identified that associate with Atx2 with the proximity and stability required for Atx2-linked enzymatic editing of the mRNA.
source: This method led to the identification of 256 Drosophila brain mRNAs that associate with Atx2 with the proximity and stability required for Atx2-linked enzymatic editing of the mRNA.
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: The identified mRNAs are reproducibly identified in replicate experiments and do not show any over-representation of highly expressed mRNAs.
source: These mRNAs are reproducibly identified in replicate experiments and do not show any over-representation of highly expressed mRNAs.
evidence: This is data from the TRIBE experiments.

claim: A substantial fraction of TRIBE-identified mRNAs either have AREs in their 3′UTRs and/or show altered steady-state levels following Atx2 knockdown.
source: Moreover, the observation that a substantial fraction of these mRNAs either have AREs in their 3′UTRs and/or show altered steady-state levels following Atx2 knockdown argues that the majority represent real Atx2 targets and not non-specific proximity-based editing events that can sometimes occur within RNP complexes (Biswas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is data from ARE analysis and RNAseq experiments.

claim: A striking enhancement of mRNAs encoding specific neuropeptides and neuronal hormones suggests that altered intercellular communication mediated by their translational regulation may contribute to behavioral plasticity.
source: For instance, a striking enhancement of mRNAs encoding specific neuropeptides and neuronal hormones suggests that altered intercellular communication mediated by their translational regulation may contribute to the behavioral plasticity associated with circadian time or long-term memory.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Gene Ontology analysis of TRIBE targets.

claim: CaMKII and per were not identified by TRIBE.
source: It is notable that two of the best-established Atx2 targets, CaMKII and per, were not identified by TRIBE.
evidence: This is an observation from the TRIBE data.

claim: CaMKII is a highly expressed mRNA that co-immunoprecipitates with Atx2.
source: While the per–Atx2 interactions, being time- and cell-type restricted (Lim and Allada, 2013; Zhang et al., 2013), could potentially be missed for statistical reasons, this is unlikely the case for CaMKII, a highly expressed mRNA that co-immunoprecipitates with Atx2 (Sudhakaran et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: CaMKII and per represent Atx2 targets missed by TRIBE because they are regulated through relatively indirect mechanisms that do not require close contact between Atx2 and the mRNA.
source: We suggest instead that these represent Atx2 targets missed by TRIBE because they are regulated through relatively indirect mechanisms that do not require close contact between Atx2 and the mRNA.
evidence: This is speculation to explain why known targets were not identified by TRIBE.

claim: For per, its 3′UTR is recognized by the sequence-specific RBP Twentyfour (TYF), which recruits Atx2 that in turns recruits a Lsm12-containing complex to the per 3′UTR, thus allowing translational activation.
source: For instance, in case of per, its 3′UTR is recognized by the sequence-specific RBP Twentyfour (TYF), which recruits Atx2 that in turns recruits a Lsm12-containing complex to the per 3′UTR, thus allowing translational activation (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: For CaMKII, Atx2 may be recruited by miRNA pathway components and act via co-regulators such as Me31B/DDX6, through mechanisms that do not rely on close proximity between Atx2 and target mRNAs.
source: Similarly, for CaMKII, Atx2 may be recruited by miRNA pathway components and act via co-regulators such as Me31B/DDX6, through mechanisms that do not rely on close proximity between Atx2 and target mRNAs.
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of Atx2 function.

claim: Atx2 directly or indirectly associates with AREs to protect mRNAs from degradation through a mechanism similar to that described previously for HuR.
source: This could be achieved by blocking ARE-dependent recruitment of RNA degradation complexes through a mechanism similar to that described previously for HuR (Peng et al., 1998).
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of ARE regulation.

claim: Physical interactions between mammalian Atxn2 and AREs have been described previously using PAR-CLIP analyses from cultured HEK293 cells.
source: These conclusions may also be relevant for mammalian Atxn2 as physical interactions between mammalian Atxn2 and AREs have been described previously using PAR-CLIP analyses from cultured HEK293 cells (Yokoshi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Atxn2-CAG100-KnockIn mouse engineered to express polyQ expanded forms of Atxn2 show a predominant upregulation of mRNAs.
source: Moreover, Atxn2-CAG100-KnockIn mouse engineered to express polyQ expanded forms of Atxn2 that should enhance granule formation show a predominant upregulation of mRNAs, consistent with a role for Atx2-mediated mRNP assembly in stabilizing target mRNAs (Sen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Individual mRNPs may be substantially remodeled as they assemble into higher order mRNP assemblies.
source: Our work provides two insights into the mechanisms of mRNP formation. First, it indicates that individual mRNPs may be substantially remodeled as they assemble into higher order mRNP assemblies.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cIDR deletion prevents both granule formation and mRNA editing.

claim: Atx2 lacking its cIDR, which cannot form granules, is also not associated closely enough with mRNAs to allow their editing by a linked ADAR catalytic domain.
source: In support of this, we show that Atx2 lacking its cIDR, which cannot form granules, is also not associated closely enough with mRNAs to allow their editing by a linked ADAR catalytic domain.
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with cIDR deletion.

claim: mRNP remodeling may be driven by major conformational changes in RBPs, which not only increase their propensity to drive mRNP condensation but also result in altered RBP–RBP and RBP–RNA interactions.
source: One possibility is that mRNP remodeling is driven by major conformational changes in RBPs, which not only increase their propensity to drive mRNP condensation but also result in altered RBP–RBP and RBP–RNA interactions.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of mRNP remodeling.

claim: G3BP/Rin exists in two dramatically different conformational states: a closed form, in which its IDRs are inaccessible for condensation reactions, and a dephosphorylation-induced open form, capable of mediating SG association.
source: In this context, recent work on G3BP/Rin has shown that the protein exists in two dramatically different conformational states: a closed form, in which its IDRs are inaccessible for condensation reactions, and a dephosphorylation-induced open form, capable of mediating SG association (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Laver et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP/Rin.

claim: Atx2 interactions with RBPs and mRNAs could be altered under conditions that support granule assembly.
source: In such a framework, it is easy to see how Atx2 interactions with RBPs and mRNAs could be altered under conditions that support granule assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the G3BP/Rin model.

claim: Alterations in the Atx2 protein itself probably occur and contribute to driving granule assembly.
source: While these changes in Atx2 interactions could occur due to structural changes in other components of Atx2-containing mRNPs, our second insight is that alterations in the Atx2 protein itself probably occur and contribute to driving granule assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the domain deletion experiments showing opposing roles of Lsm and cIDR.

claim: Ataxin-2 is a modular protein capable of association with multiple translational control components.
source: Ataxin-2 is a modular protein capable of association with multiple translational control components (Dansithong et al., 2015; Lastres-Becker et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Satterfield and Pallanck, 2006; Swisher and Parker, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Homology-based modeling studies and indirect experimental observations have suggested that the Lsm domain of Atx2 may mediate RNA interaction.
source: Although Atx2 lacks RNA recognition domains like RRMs, KH, or other previously characterized RNA-binding domains, homology-based modeling studies and indirect experimental observations have suggested that the Lsm domain of Atx2 may mediate RNA interaction (Calabretta and Richard, 2015; Hentze et al., 2018; Yokoshi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Direct experimental tests show that close Atx2 interactions with mRNA, as assessed by TRIBE, are actively prevented by the Lsm domain, which also opposes mRNP assembly.
source: However, direct experimental tests of this hypothesis show that close Atx2 interactions with mRNA, as assessed by TRIBE, are actively prevented by the Lsm domain, which also opposes mRNP assembly (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is data from TRIBE and cell biological experiments.

claim: The cIDR that drives mRNP assembly is necessary for Atx2-coupled editing of target mRNA.
source: In contrast, the cIDR that drives mRNP assembly is necessary for Atx2-coupled editing of target mRNA.
evidence: This is data from TRIBE experiments with cIDR deletion.

claim: Atx2 association with individual, potentially translationally active mRNPs in the soluble phases is mediated by Lsm domain–RBP interactions that also occlude or prevent cIDR-mediated mRNP assembly.
source: The simplest explanation for these findings is that Atx2 association with individual, potentially translationally active mRNPs in the soluble phases is mediated by Lsm domain–RBP interactions that also occlude or prevent cIDR-mediated mRNP assembly (Ciosk et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2017; Satterfield and Pallanck, 2006).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the data.

claim: Conditions that promote mRNP assembly disrupt Lsm-domain-mediated interactions and enable cIDR-driven granule formation.
source: Conditions that promote mRNP assembly disrupt Lsm-domain-mediated interactions and enable cIDR-driven granule formation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed to explain the data.

claim: Recent work on G3BP has elaborated phosphorylation-regulated intramolecular interactions that allow the molecule to switch between soluble and assembly-competent conformations.
source: We note that recent work on G3BP has beautifully elaborated phosphorylation-regulated intramolecular interactions that similarly allow the molecule to switch between soluble and assembly-competent conformations (Guillén-Boixet et al., 2020; Laver et al., 2020; Sanders et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on G3BP.

claim: Regulation of intermolecular interactions mediated by the Lsm domain will be involved in control of Atx2-mediated granule assembly.
source: Though our experiments do not yet define molecular and biophysical details by which Atx2 transitions from assembly-inhibited to assembly-competent states, our observations (1) clearly demonstrate crucial opposing, physiological roles of the Lsm and cIDR domains in this process and (2) suggest that regulation of intermolecular interactions mediated by the Lsm domain will be involved in control of Atx2-mediated granule assembly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data.

claim: Ataxin-2 has additional essential functions beyond those described in the study.
source: It is important to note that Ataxin-2 has additional essential functions beyond those described here.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that structured domains are essential for viability but not required for TRIBE-target binding.

claim: A class of Atx2-target mRNAs is likely regulated outside of mRNP granules through largely structured-domain interactions.
source: In particular, given that the Atx2 structured domains not required for TRIBE-target binding are essential for survival, unlike the IDR, which is required for editing of TRIBE targets but not for animal survival, it appears likely that a class of Atx2-target mRNAs is regulated outside of mRNP granules through largely structured-domain interactions (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the genetic and TRIBE data.

claim: Assembly-promoting mutations in the Ataxin-2 gene or associated RNA binding and SG proteins such as TDP-43 can cause neurodegenerative disease.
source: Ataxin-2 has attracted considerable clinical interest for three main reasons. First, assembly-promoting mutations in the Ataxin-2 gene or associated RNA binding and SG proteins such as TDP-43 can cause neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: SG proteins such as TDP-43 are usually present in cytoplasmic protein inclusions associated with familial and heritable forms of ALS and FTD.
source: Second, SG proteins such as TDP-43 are usually present in cytoplasmic protein inclusions associated with familial and heritable forms of ALS and FTD.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Reduction of Ataxin-2 can slow neurodegeneration in animal models of ALS.
source: Third, reduction of Ataxin-2 can slow neurodegeneration in animal models of ALS, indicating that the normal function of Ataxin-2 is required for initiation or progression of disease (Becker et al., 2017; Scoles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The normal function of Ataxin-2 is required for initiation or progression of ALS disease.
source: Third, reduction of Ataxin-2 can slow neurodegeneration in animal models of ALS, indicating that the normal function of Ataxin-2 is required for initiation or progression of disease (Becker et al., 2017; Scoles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that reducing Ataxin-2 slows disease progression.

claim: Therapeutics based on reducing levels of Ataxin-2 are being developed by major companies such as Ionis and Biogen Inc.
source: These findings, interpreted in a framework wherein SGs are thought to facilitate the nucleation of pathogenic amyloid filaments, have led to the development of therapeutics based on reducing levels of Ataxin-2, for example, using antisense oligonucleotides by major companies such as Ionis and Biogen Inc.
evidence: This is factual information about therapeutic development.

claim: Mutations inactivating the Lsm domain could have effects similar to polyQ expansions and promote disease.
source: In this context, the discovery that the Lsm domain inhibits mRNP assembly suggests, first, that mutations inactivating this domain could have effects similar to polyQ expansions and promote disease
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding that Lsm inhibits granule assembly.

claim: Compounds targeting specific domains and activities of Ataxin-2 may prove more effective as therapeutics than those that knock down protein levels.
source: and, second, that compounds targeting specific domains and activities of Ataxin-2 may prove more effective as therapeutics than those that knock down protein levels.
evidence: This is speculation about therapeutic strategies based on the study's findings.

claim: Ataxin-2 protein has several important roles not only in mRNA stabilization but also in protein translation, cell signaling, metabolism, and embryonic development.
source: The case for our understanding of the function of each Atx2 domain and developing specific modulators is particularly strong since Ataxin-2 protein itself has several important roles not only in mRNA stabilization, as shown here, but also in protein translation, cell signaling, metabolism, and embryonic development (Halbach et al., 2017; Inagaki et al., 2020; Kato et al., 2019; Lim and Allada, 2013; Meierhofer et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2019; Yokoshi et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.
